results.desc: Anjali, 34, Chennai, Catholic. Their third round of IVF failed two weeks ago, and she has stopped going to her cousin's baby shower and the family WhatsApp group because every message is about the new baby. She still goes to Mass, but lately she sits there feeling that God said no without telling her why.

answers.wanted: Grieving; also something like 'jealous' or 'left out', which I'd be ashamed to say but is true
Wanting a child / something I've been waiting and praying for. I didn't lose a person, I lost a hope, so 'lost' felt only half right
Kind, but they're all happy about something that hurts me. 'Hard to be around' sounds like I'm blaming them, and they've done nothing wrong
He answered, but the answer was no and He won't say why. 'Nothing changes' is near, but it isn't silence, it's a refusal

friction.note: No option for infertility, pregnancy or waiting for a child, even though that's something a lot of women would come here with. 'My health' is too clinical and 'Someone or something I've lost' is unclear: does a failed IVF round count as a loss? I hesitated.
There's nothing between 'Fine/Kind' and 'Hard to be around' for 'they're lovely, but their joy hurts me'. 'Hard to be around' makes it sound like the fault is theirs, which feels unfair to my family.

'Silent. I pray and nothing changes' assumes God hasn't acted. What I actually feel is that He did answer, and the answer was no. An option like 'He said no' or 'He's said no and I don't know why' would fit.
There's no word for grief, only 'Sad', which feels too small two weeks after this. Envy or jealousy isn't there either, and it's the feeling I'm most ashamed of.
'Something hard just happened' is fine, but two weeks on it's also 'getting worse' as the baby messages keep coming. Letting me pick two would help.

results.overall: It was quick and mostly gentle, and 'Why?' as a thing to say to God hit exactly. But nothing in it named what I'm actually going through (wanting a child and being told no), so I ended up choosing near misses and wondering whether the psalm would really be about me.

verdict.why: As Anjali, I would say yes to the first line. The heaviness from the third failed round hasn't lifted in two weeks, and I would know that line was about me. Psalm 42 is a strong result for me. It says "why have You forgotten me", and it describes people asking "where is your God?" while the psalmist keeps going to the house of God. That is almost exactly me at Mass, feeling that God said no and never told me why. The psalm asks "Why are you downcast?" twice without ever answering. That keeps it honest: it lets me stay unresolved while still pointing me to hope, and it doesn't tell me what I should feel. It would speak to me, not hurt me. Its one weakness is that "weighed down or uneasy" is too mild for grief. It reads like a bad week, not a loss, so I'd only say yes after a pause. A line with a word like "grief" or "loss" in it, or "you feel God has gone quiet", would have made me feel truly seen. The line doesn't box me in, and I'm glad it doesn't mention children or babies. The fallback route would also have worked, since "it's weighing on me, and it won't lift" leads to the same psalm.
verdict.wouldHurt: Athanasius's promise that "what grieves you is healed" could land as a quick fix two weeks after a failed IVF round. It hints that singing the psalm will make the grief go away, when what I need is permission to stay in it. Also, "uneasy" undersells what I'm going through: I'm grieving, not uneasy. If the full result ever added a psalm about God giving the barren woman a home (Psalm 113:9), it would wound me badly right now.
verdict.theirSituation: She is grieving a third failed IVF round and pulling away from family baby news, and she keeps going to Mass while feeling that God has said no and stayed silent.

results.desc: Dale, 52, Dayton, Ohio, grew up Baptist and drifted. He had three years sober and drank again last Friday after a bad week at the plant, and he has not told his sponsor or his wife yet. He keeps thinking God must be done with him, though some part of him wants to call someone before it happens again.

answers.wanted: I messed up. Something I did just happened, not something that happened to me.
They don't know yet. I'm hiding it from them.
Done with me. Like I used up my last chance.
I'm sorry, and help me not do it again. Would have tapped both sorry and help.

friction.note: Every option reads as something done to you or something going on around you. 'Something hard just happened' is close enough, but a relapse is something he did. He would pause over it.

Nothing covers people who don't know. His wife and sponsor are 'fine' only because he hasn't told them. 'Upset with me, and with reason' is what he fears, not what is true yet. Tapping 'Fine' feels like one more lie.

'Displeased with me' is softer than what he actually thinks, which is that God has given up on him. A man who drifted from a Baptist upbringing will notice that gap. There is no 'He must be done with me' option.
With only one pick, he has to choose between confessing and asking for help, and for him they go together. The feelings question lets him pick two; this one could too.
'A sense that God is warning me' could sound preachy or threatening to someone already ashamed. 'Something I keep going back to' fits a relapse well and doesn't lecture him, which is good.
The key 'heavy' shows as 'Sad', which is fine. There is no 'Guilty' option, but 'Ashamed' covers it.

results.overall: It was quick, and for the most part it didn't feel preachy. The 'Fine on the outside' and 'Something I keep going back to' answers made him feel seen. It fell short in three places: it has no words for a secret nobody knows yet, God only gets 'displeased' when he fears 'done with me', and he could say sorry or ask for help but not both. What he'll judge is whether the result speaks to mercy and to making that call.

verdict.why: As Dale, I'd tap "Yes, that's it" on the first line. I drank after three years, I know it was wrong, I'm hiding it and ashamed of it, and part of me wants to come back. That describes me without making me say "relapse" or "alcohol" out loud, which I wouldn't want to do on a website. Psalm 51 answers my real fear, which is that God must be done with me. It opens on His great compassion. 51:7 says I can be washed clean. Reading on, I'd reach "do not cast me from Your presence" and "a broken and contrite heart You will not despise", which say almost word for word what I'm scared of and then answer it. It would land. Athanasius's wording, "you are turning back, and you are asking for mercy", treats me as someone already on the way back, not a lost cause. That's a mercy. Line 2 (a warning from God that is shaking me) is close but reads as fear of punishment, not what I did. Line 3 misses.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounds, but two things sit slightly off. "You've done wrong" is a moral frame. It fits how I feel, but it gives my relapse no name and no sense of a slip after years of fighting. A line like "you slipped after holding on a long time" would feel even more like me. The bigger gap: the result is all between me and God. Nothing nudges me toward the thing I half want to do, which is call my sponsor or tell my wife before it happens again. Psalm 51:13 ("then I will teach transgressors Your ways") hints at going back to people, but the page doesn't draw that out. "Whiter than snow" could also let me think the matter is settled privately, so I skip telling anyone. A gentle "confession to God often goes with telling someone you trust" would help. For someone like me, a recovery or helpline pointer would help more here than 988. The Bathsheba heading on Psalm 51, if it's shown, is a little jarring (adultery isn't my sin), but I'd read past it.
verdict.theirSituation: A sober alcoholic drank again after three years, is hiding it from his sponsor and wife, fears God has given up on him, and half wants to reach out before he drinks again.

results.desc: Helen, 47, Leeds, Church of England. Her mum has dementia and moved in with her in the spring; most nights Helen is up twice because her mum wanders and does not always know who she is. She is short with her teenagers and feels guilty about it, and prayer has shrunk to 'please just get me through today'.

answers.wanted: Same grind, slowly getting worse. Mum's dementia is progressing, but nothing new has happened
Worn out and Guilty. There's no 'Guilty', and 'Ashamed' is too strong for snapping at the kids
'They need a lot from me' or 'I've been hard on them'. The problem is her being short with them, not them being hard to be around
'I've barely had time for Him'. He's not far or silent, prayer has just shrunk to one line
'Just get me through today.' 'Help' and 'I'm so tired' both fit, and she'd have liked to pick both
'How I've been with my family'. It isn't one thing she did, it's how she keeps snapping, but 'Something I keep going back to' sounds like a vice or addiction

friction.note: No 'Guilty' option. 'Ashamed' feels too heavy for a stretched carer who is short with her teenagers, so she has to skip her main feeling or overstate it.
'Upset with me, and with reason' reads a bit like an accusation. Nothing covers people who depend on you or need caring for, and 'Hard to be around' feels unkind to say about a mum with dementia.
She'd have wanted to pick two here, since 'Someone I love' and 'Someone or something I've lost' both fit (losing her mum while she's still alive). One pick only feels like a box.

'Something I keep going back to' sounds like addiction or a secret sin. 'A sense that God is warning me' might unsettle someone who is just exhausted, and it hints the quiz sees her tiredness as a moral failing.
Nothing for 'I've no time or energy for Him', which is different from drifting or having Him in the background. 'I've drifted from Him' would make her feel guiltier.
There's no plain caregiving or 'looking after someone' option anywhere in the quiz, and that is the whole of her life right now.

results.overall: Quick and mostly gentle, and 'Someone I love' then 'I'm losing them' landed hard in a good way. But she kept hitting options that were nearly right. The quiz has no word for guilt or for caring for someone, so she worried it would read her tiredness as sin rather than as an overloaded life.

verdict.why: Helen's life is wearing her down. She is up every night with her mum, she has no reserves left, and all she can pray is "get me through today." Line 2 says that exactly: "worn you down", "you need comfort." Psalm 102:4 ("withered like grass; I even forget to eat my bread") fits a carer who skips meals. 102:17, "He will not despise their prayer," answers her fear that her tiny prayers don't count. She would reject line 1. She does feel guilty for snapping at her teenagers, but she has not turned away from God and doesn't need to come back. Line 3 is close, but it's about the soul being uneasy, and what she feels is depleted.
verdict.wouldHurt: Line 1 comes first, as the best match. For a woman who is caring for her mother at great cost, being met first with "You've done wrong... you're ashamed" would sting. It turns her guilt about being short-tempered into a charge of sin, and she may feel judged before she reaches the line that fits. "Empty and listless" is also slightly off. She isn't listless. She is running flat out on nothing. "Exhausted" or "running on empty" would fit her better.
verdict.theirSituation: She is a carer worn out by her mother's dementia and broken sleep. She feels guilty for being short with her children and has no strength left to pray more than "get me through today."

results.desc: Chinedu, 29, Lagos, Pentecostal. His business partner emptied their joint account and is now telling their suppliers and even people at church that Chinedu was the one who stole. He is angry, can hardly sleep, and keeps asking God why the man telling lies is doing fine while he looks like the thief.

answers.wanted: Both 'Something hard just happened' and 'Getting worse': the theft happened, and now the lies keep spreading
'Someone betrayed me and stole from me'. It is about people and money at the same time
'He's letting this happen', or 'Watching, but not stepping in yet'. He knows God is there, but God is not acting
'Why?' and 'It isn't fair' were near-ties. A pick-two would have let him say all of it
'A business partner I trusted' plus 'people at my church'. He could only pick one, and the church gossip is a big part of the hurt
'No, but it's reached my church'. The attack is not about his faith, but his church life is caught up in it
'That people believe him' would be sharper. Being taken for the thief is the core of it

friction.note: His loudest question, why the liar is doing fine, never gets asked. 'Bad people doing well' is behind focus=world or say=unfair, and he tapped 'Clear my name'. An accused person who taps 'Clear my name' should probably see that follow-up too.
'Money' and 'People in my life' are separate choices, but for him the theft and the betrayal are the same thing. Forcing one choice feels like a box.
There is no option for 'lying about me' or 'blaming me for what they did'. 'Talking about me' sounds like light gossip, not slander.
'Is your faith part of it?' is easy to misread. His church is caught up in it, but not because of what he believes. He might tap 'Partly' for the wrong reason.
Single choice. A partner plus a church crowd is two groups, and 'Friends, or people I trusted' does not quite say 'business partner'.
'Silent. I pray and nothing changes' fits well enough, but a Pentecostal might not like calling God 'silent'. 'Not acting yet' would feel less like doubt.

results.overall: Quick, and it mostly felt like it was about his real situation. The 'Clear my name' option especially felt like it understood him. His biggest gripe: he never got to say what eats at him most, that the liar is doing well, and slander or theft does not appear in the options except as 'talking about me'.

verdict.why: Line 1 describes my situation. The man spreading lies about me was my partner and my friend. Now suppliers and people at church are hearing his story, and I lie awake going over it. Psalm 55:13 hit me hardest: "it is you, a man like myself, my companion and close friend". That is exactly him. I would tap "Yes, that's it" straight away. The psalm also speaks to my anger and my lost sleep. It has the smooth words that hide a drawn sword, the wish to fly away, and "cast your burden on the LORD". The advice to keep praising God while it goes round in my head fits too. Line 2 is also me: I want God to judge between us, and I have walked with integrity. But line 1 is closer. What none of the three lines names is the question I keep asking God: why is the liar doing fine while I look like the thief? That is Psalm 37 or 73 ground. As far as I know, Athanasius's letter pairs those psalms with seeing the wicked prosper. So the quiz found my wound, but not my question.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounds. A few things are slightly off. "People you thought were your friends" is plural and "others are piling on" sounds like a crowd, but mine is one partner, and the others are people he is misleading. The advice says the slander "grieves" me, but I am angry more than grieved. Psalm 55 also asks for death to come on the enemy. For an angry man that could feed the anger unless the quiet note about hard words is kept with it. Finally, no line asks about the money he stole, or about the wicked doing well.
verdict.theirSituation: A friend and business partner betrayed me: he stole our money and now lies that I am the thief, even at church. I am angry, I cannot sleep, and I keep asking God why the liar does well while I carry the blame.

results.desc: Bea, 16, Quezon City, Catholic. A friend screenshotted something private Bea said about another girl and shared it, and now half her class has left her out of the group chat and people laugh when she walks past. She does not want to go to school, and when she prays she mostly cries and wonders whether God even notices things like this.

answers.wanted: Both 'something hard just happened' and 'getting worse': it happened last week and the laughing keeps going
Embarrassed or humiliated. 'Ashamed' sounds like I did something terrible, but I also sort of did, so I'd want a third pick
Leaving me out. And my friend turned on me too, but only two picks are allowed
I don't know if He even notices stuff like this
Do You even see this? / Do You care about this?
My classmates, and one friend I trusted. 'Work or school' works, but it sounds like it's for adults

friction.note: There's no 'leaving me out / ignoring me', which is the main thing happening to her. 'Upset with me, and with reason' comes close to her part in it, but she wouldn't want to admit that next to 'making fun of me'. Only two picks, when mocking, talking and one friend turning on her all apply.
There's no 'Embarrassed' or 'Humiliated'. 'Ashamed' feels heavy and moral, like calling yourself a bad person, so a teen avoids it even when part of it fits.
Her real question is whether God cares about small-seeming things like school drama. 'Far away', 'Silent' and 'I'm not sure He's there' all miss the 'does He notice this' feeling.
'Clear my name.' doesn't fit because she did say the thing. There's nothing like 'Do You see me?'. With 15 options the list is long to scroll on a phone.
'People at work or school' and 'People with power over me' read like options written for adults. A teen would want to see 'classmates'.
'Is your faith part of it?' is a little confusing when the conflict has nothing to do with religion. Answering 'No' is easy, though.
'What they might be planning' and 'Feeling trapped' sound dramatic for a school situation. 'Being pushed out' fit well.

results.overall: It went quickly and mostly felt like it got her: 'Really hard', 'People in my life' and 'Being pushed out' landed. But the most painful parts of her situation (being left out, being embarrassed, knowing she partly caused it, wondering whether God cares about something this 'small') had no exact option, so she kept tapping near-misses.

verdict.why: Being dropped from the group chat and laughed at in the hallway really does feel like being driven out and left on my own, so I'd tap yes on the first line. The advice says not to be afraid as if I were alone, because God is with me there. That goes straight at what I keep asking when I pray: whether He even notices. Psalm 63's "dry and weary land" and "my soul thirsts for You" also sound like crying through my prayers. Psalm 42 would have been my second choice, but it's more about a general heaviness and says nothing about the people who turned on me.
verdict.wouldHurt: "People set against you" and "persecution" make me sound completely innocent, and I'm not. I really did say something mean about that girl. Part of what hurts is the shame, not only the unfairness. Being called persecuted could feel hollow, as if the quiz didn't really get my situation, or it could let me skip past my own part. Some readers in my place would feel accused if they read "persecution" as an ironic comment on them. The line fits me more than it doesn't, but nothing in it touches the guilt.
verdict.theirSituation: A 16-year-old whose friend leaked a mean private remark of hers is now shut out and mocked at school. She's hurt partly by her own fault, is dreading school, and wonders whether God notices something this small.

results.desc: Mihai, 61, Bucharest, Orthodox. He guaranteed a loan for his son's business, the business closed, and now the bank is coming after Mihai's savings and maybe the flat. He lights a candle every Sunday and says the prayers, but he is ashamed to tell his wife how bad the numbers are and feels God is very far off.

answers.wanted: Money, but because of my son: both 'Money' and 'Someone I love' at once. It is his son's debt that is taking his savings and maybe the flat.

'I'm hiding something from them' or 'I can't face them'. His wife is kind and his son isn't against him; the one against him is the bank, and nothing here fits a creditor or his own silence toward his wife.
'Something I'm hiding from someone I love' (not telling his wife how bad it is). Signing the guarantee was a decision, not really a sin, so 'Something I did' is only near enough.

friction.note: Every option is about how others treat him. There is nothing for his own side of it: hiding the truth from his wife, or a bank or creditors pressing him. 'Against me' would be the bank, but that could send him into questions about enemies and faith that don't fit. He ends up tapping 'Fine', which hides the real trouble.

Only one pick, and money and his son are the same worry here. No follow-up asks about money (debt, losing the home, being responsible for someone else's debt), so the quiz never hears what the trouble actually is.

Picking 'Ashamed' brings up a question that treats shame as guilt or sin ('Something I keep going back to', 'Where my thoughts have taken me', 'A sense that God is warning me'). His shame is about failing his family and keeping a secret, not about sin. 'A sense that God is warning me' could feel like being pushed into a box, or a bit preachy, to a man who already fears God is far off.
Fine overall. A man his age might look for 'Worried' rather than 'Anxious' and would use 'Afraid' instead, which works.
'Far away' fits well. Some Orthodox users might notice there is no option like 'I keep praying but my heart isn't in it', which is between 'drift' and 'far', but this is minor.

results.overall: The quiz was quick and mostly easy for Mihai. The mood, God and 'Help.' questions spoke to him directly. It lost him on the people and shame questions, though: his trouble is a debt he took on for his son and is hiding from his wife, and the options only covered people turning on him or sins he committed. So the answers he gave leave out the center of his situation.

verdict.why: Line 1 would get "Not quite". He is ashamed, but of the numbers and of hiding them from his wife. He did not sin: he stood guarantor for his son out of love. "You've done wrong... and you want to come back" reads as if helping his son was a fall, and he has not left God either, since he lights the candle every Sunday. Line 2 is true enough: he is afraid of losing his savings and the flat, and he needs something to hold on to. "What can man do to me?" lands when the one after him is a bank. But the line catches only the fear. It misses the two things that weigh most on him: the shame he hides from his wife and the feeling that God is far away. The fallback's "It's weighing on me, and it won't lift" (Psalm 42: "Why are you downcast, O my soul... where is your God?") would fit him more deeply, but he says yes to line 2 before he ever sees it. That is a sign the ordering and the fallback deserve a look for people like him.
verdict.wouldHurt: Psalm 118 is a psalm of triumph ("The LORD is on my side; I will not be afraid"). To a man who feels God is very far off, that confidence can feel like being told he should not be afraid, which is a quiet rebuke. The Athanasius line "whatever in you is afraid is strengthened by hope" is gentle and helps. A smaller point: he knows these as Psalm 50 and 117 (Septuagint numbering), and his prayer book says "Psalm 50" daily. Western numbers with no Orthodox number beside them feel slightly foreign. The first line he passed over could also sting a little on the way, as if his generosity were being called sin.
verdict.theirSituation: A faithful older man is losing his savings and maybe his home over a debt he guaranteed for his son. He is afraid, but even more he is ashamed and hiding it from his wife, and he feels abandoned by God.

results.desc: Kristen, 38, Fort Worth, Texas, lapsed Baptist. Her divorce is being finalised this month and she is splitting the week with her ex over their two kids, which leaves her alone in a quiet house every other weekend. She has started to pray again for the first time in years, mostly asking God whether it was her fault.

answers.wanted: Something is ending right now (the divorce is being finalised this month). It is neither 'just happened' nor 'finally over'.
Lonely, and 'Guilty' or 'Wondering if it was my fault'. Ashamed is heavier than what she feels.
Something like 'It's complicated' or 'Some kind, some hard'. Her ex is hard to be around, her kids are gone every other weekend, and her friends are fine.
'I'm finding my way back to Him' or 'I've just started talking to Him again'. She did drift, but she is praying again now.
'Was it my fault?' That is the exact prayer she has been praying.
'I don't know if it was my fault.' 'Something I did' admits blame, and 'It's not something I did' answers the very thing she is asking God.

friction.note: There is no option for something hard that is ending right now, like a divorce being finalised. The choices sort things into just happened, the same, or over.
'Ashamed' is the only word near guilt. A divorced lapsed Baptist may flinch at being boxed into shame. 'Guilty' or 'Blaming myself' would fit better.
You can pick only one or two, but her circle is mixed (ex, kids, friends). Nothing names an ex or a split family, and 'Far away, or gone' for her kids on alternate weekends feels grim.
'I've drifted from Him' is stuck in the past for someone who has just started praying again. There is no 'coming back' option here, though the good follow-up has one.

'It's not something I did. I just feel it.' reads as the quiz answering her question for her, and 'I just feel it' can sound dismissive. There is no 'I don't know if it was me' option. 'A sense that God is warning me' could unsettle someone raised Baptist who is already afraid she is to blame.
No option carries self-blame without admitting it ('Was it me?'). 'I'm sorry.' presumes guilt, and 'Why?' is only close.

results.overall: It felt quick and mostly human. She could find herself in most screens, but the quiz kept making her either admit fault or deny it. The one thing she is actually asking ("was it my fault?") never had its own option.

verdict.why: As Kristen I'd tap "Yes, that's it" on the first line. It describes how I feel in the quiet house on my weekends without the kids, and it doesn't make me name the divorce. Psalm 42 fits someone who has just started praying again after years away. It is about a soul that is downcast and thirsty for God and asks "why", and that is what my prayers have been. I'd find it comforting to read the lines "Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him" twice. The line doesn't touch my real question, whether the divorce was my fault, so it describes me near enough but not exactly. Still, I'm glad it didn't hand me a repentance psalm like Psalm 51. That would have answered my question with "yes". Line 2 would have felt off. God hasn't slipped into the background for me; I'm reaching for Him again. The fallback's "It's weighing on me, and it won't lift" would also have led to Psalm 42, so the quiz lands in the same place either way.
verdict.theirSituation: She is newly divorced and alone every other weekend, and has started praying again mostly to ask whether the divorce was her fault. So guilt and loneliness sit under the unease that line 1 names.

results.desc: Jae-won, 24, Seoul, Presbyterian. A bad Crohn's flare put him in hospital twice this year and he has had to drop out of his master's programme while his friends move ahead. His parents' church friends keep saying they are praying for healing, and he is tired of being the sick one and quietly angry at God.

answers.wanted: Something like 'It keeps coming back': a long illness is not the same or worse, it flares and settles and flares again
My health AND falling behind everyone my age; 'What's next for me' was the other half and I could only pick one
'They mean well, but it isn't helping' or 'Everyone treats me as the sick one'. They are kind, and that is exactly what wears me out
'Why me?' or 'Why haven't You healed me?'; 'Why?' alone felt too vague, 'How long?' was a near second

Nothing here fits well; my 'unfair' was about my own body and my life stalling while friends move ahead, not about the world. 'Something that happened to me' is the nearest, but illness is not really something that 'happened' once, it is ongoing

friction.note: I tapped 'It isn't fair' because I'm sick and falling behind, and then got asked 'What gets to you most?' about bad people doing well and Christians being persecuted. It felt like the quiz had misread me, and 'Something that happened to me' was the only way out. It needs an illness or a 'my own life' option, or it shouldn't fire from 'unfair' alone when focus is health.

There's no option for well-meaning people who wear you down. 'Kind to me' sounds like I'm grateful, and 'Hard to be around' sounds like I'm blaming people who are praying for me. That's the exact tension I'm living in, and I couldn't say it.
'Upset with me, and with reason' felt a bit like the quiz fishing for guilt. It's harmless, but in a list about other people it stood out.
None of the options describe a chronic illness that flares. 'About the same' undersells two hospital stays.
You can only pick one, but health and 'what's next for me' are tangled together for me. Other questions let you pick two, so this one could too.

'Thank You.', 'How great You are.' and 'Make me who You want me to be.' are fine to have, but next to how I feel they read a little like the answers I'm supposed to want to give. Being able to say 'It isn't fair' was a relief. Please don't let the result turn around and scold me for it or tell me to praise anyway.
'Silent. I pray and nothing changes' was the best line in the quiz. It fitted exactly, especially with everyone around me praying for healing.

results.overall: It was quick, and most questions let me be honest, including being angry at God, which I didn't expect a Christian site to allow. But being sick for a long time and watching everyone move on without me has almost nowhere to go: the world follow-up and the people options kept pushing me into boxes that were about other people or the world, not my own body and stalled life. I'd be wary that the psalm at the end gets it.

verdict.why: He would tap yes, though not straight away. "Worn down" fits: two hospital stays, a dropped degree, friends moving ahead. But "empty and listless, and you need comfort" misses what he mostly feels, which is quiet anger at God. He isn't asking for comfort. He's tired of people offering it. He says yes because nothing closer is on offer, and the fallback leads to Psalm 102 anyway. The psalm is where it lands. Verse 10 ("You have lifted me up and thrown me down") speaks his anger at God for him. Verses 23-24 (God has broken his strength and cut his days short partway through his life) describe a 24-year-old whose life stopped while his friends' lives went on. Verse 7, the lonely bird on the housetop, is how being "the sick one" feels. The printed text reads him better than the tag line does.
verdict.wouldHurt: "Where it turns: He will turn toward the prayer of the destitute" is shown up front. To him it could read like the "we're praying for your healing" line he is tired of, a quick move to reassurance before his complaint has been heard. "And you need comfort" makes him sound passive and needy when he is angry. Nothing on the page says anger at God is allowed. The psalm itself says it, in verse 10, but the summary lines don't point to it. verdict.theirSituation: He is a young man with a chronic illness whose life has been cut short in the middle of his studies. He is more angry at God than empty, and sick of hearing about healing.

results.desc: Grace, 71, Kisumu, Kenya, Anglican. Years ago she was harsh and cold to her daughter-in-law, and now her son rarely visits and her grandchildren barely know her. I don't know if He has forgiven me

results.overall: The questions were quick and gentle, and 'I'm sorry.' and 'Ashamed' let her say what she has never said aloud, which would move her. She had to press her situation into nearby options at three points: an old wrong against family, a family that stays away rather than being upset, and wondering whether God has forgiven her.

verdict.why: Line 1 is my situation in one breath. I was wrong, I know it, I am ashamed, and I want to come back. I would tap "Yes, that's it" at once. Psalm 51 is the psalm an Anglican woman my age already knows from Ash Wednesday. Its opening, "blot out my transgressions", is the prayer I have never said out loud. Here it is written out, so I can finally say it. The turn at 51:7, "wash me, and I will be whiter than snow", speaks to my real question: can God make me clean even if my family has not forgiven me? Athanasius's words, "you are turning back, and you are asking for mercy", treat me as someone coming home, not someone condemned. I would feel seen and not boxed in. Two small gaps. First, my wrong was against a person, my daughter-in-law, and the result speaks only of God's mercy. Nothing points me towards saying sorry to her, though that is the thing I have never done. Second, 51:4, "against You only have I sinned", could leave me thinking I only need to settle things with God. Even so, if the full psalm is printed, 51:17 ("a broken and contrite heart, O God, You will not despise") would answer what I am afraid of more directly than any line the preview shows.
verdict.wouldHurt: The blunt "You've done wrong" does not hurt her, because she already says it to herself. The small risk is 51:4 ("against You only have I sinned"). With nothing pointing back to the family she hurt, it could quietly suggest she never needs to apologise to her daughter-in-law, and she might settle for that. It would not wound her, but the result feels half-finished for someone whose sin was against a person.

Protect my family.

That they'll hurt my wife or daughter

Fear for his family, the heart of his situation, is only caught by the 'someone I love' branch.

Second, "don't give in" could read as advice not to pay the gang or to stand up to them, and following that could get someone hurt. verdict.theirSituation: A shopkeeper being extorted by a gang that has physically waited for him. He is afraid for his family, can't escape, and prays nightly for protection.

results.desc: Megan, 33, Minneapolis, Lutheran. It is a busy but fine month: a big deadline at work, two kids with colds, and the cat needed a vet visit she did not budget for. answers.wanted: Worn out fits exactly. Anxious is a bit strong; she'd have tapped something like 'Stretched thin' or 'Frazzled'
Everything at once: work, sick kids and an unexpected bill. Something like 'Too many things at once' or being able to pick two
Something lighter and practical, like 'Get me through this week' or 'Give me a quiet minute'. 'I'm so tired.' sounds heavier than she feels

'Upset with me, and with reason' is an odd phrase and takes a second read. Otherwise it's fine: 'Fine' was easy to tap.

'Just there, in the background' fits, but it may sound a little guilty to someone who chats with Him daily in the car. 'Near, but quiet' was almost as good. The two are close enough that she might hesitate.

results.overall: It was quick and mostly easy. The first two questions nailed her ('Busy, but fine', 'About the same'), but after that the options lean toward crisis and lament, so an ordinary hectic month had to be stretched a little to fit. She'd finish it, maybe wondering if her answers made her sound more worn down than she is.

verdict.why: Line 1 is too heavy for Megan. She isn't empty or listless, just busy and tired. Being told she needs comfort for a withered heart would feel like the quiz overreacted to a month of colds and deadlines, so she taps "Not quite". Line 2 is close. God hasn't gone anywhere, but He has been squeezed into the car ride to daycare between everything else, and she would like to notice Him more. Psalm 103 fits a busy but fine life well. It asks her to rouse her own soul and not forget God's kind deeds, which means counting blessings when the month is full. For a Lutheran who talks to God in the car, it's warm, not a scolding. Line 3 (weighed down, uneasy) would also be too heavy for her, and she never gets that far.
verdict.wouldHurt: "Slipped into the background" could sting a little, as if her car prayers don't count. "Wake your soul up to Him again" also suggests she has drifted, when really she is just busy. A gentler wording such as "Life is so full that God gets squeezed in at the edges" would be exactly her. Still, Psalm 103 itself reads as an invitation, not a judgment.
verdict.theirSituation: Megan is busy but fine, not in any trouble. Her faith is still there, but it has been squeezed into snatched moments in the car, and she would like it to have more room.

results.desc: Tom, 19, Birmingham, UK, christened Anglican but never really went. A friend from his course goes to church and got him curious, so he has been reading Mark's Gospel on his phone at night. He is not sure what he believes, but he is surprised it is more interesting than he expected.

This assumes he already talks to God. For a non-churchgoer, "If you could say one thing to Him" is fine as a hypothetical, but most options ("I miss You", "How great You are", "Make me who You want me to be") read like prayers from a believer. Something like "Are You real?" or "Show me" would suit newcomers.

The heading "What's behind the good?" is fine. "Coming to faith, mine or someone else's" and "Coming back to Him" feel like they're nudging toward a conversion story, but "I'm not sure yet" rescues it. Options like "His kindness, to me and to everyone" sound churchy to someone who's new.

results.overall: Quick and mostly painless on a phone. The feelings and people questions fitted him well. The God questions, though, are written for someone who already believes, so a curious 19-year-old reading Mark kept picking the nearest option rather than a true one, and felt slightly like an outsider.

verdict.why: Line 1 describes someone who used to stand firm and is slipping. Tom never had faith to slip from. He is finding his feet, not losing them, so he would tap "Not quite." Line 2 comes closer, because he is surprised something is good. But what he wonders at is a person in Mark's Gospel, not the order of the world. "How good His commands are" also assumes a belief he hasn't reached. An honest 19-year-old who is "not sure what he believes" would feel that line puts words in his mouth. The fallback is the worst of the three for him. It assumes he is "going through" something hard, and every option offered is suffering: grinding, a weight that won't lift, fear. He is simply curious and a bit intrigued. Being handed options about distress would feel like the quiz decided he must be broken. His situation, a beginner's curiosity and the first stirrings of interest, is missing from both the lines and the fallback.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounds him, but it misreads him in two ways. Psalm 73 frames him as someone backsliding. The fallback frames him as someone in trouble when he is just curious. He would probably shrug, decide the quiz is for church people, and leave.
verdict.theirSituation: He is an unchurched 19-year-old who has started reading Mark out of curiosity, finds it more interesting than he expected, and doesn't know yet what he believes. He is at the beginning, not struggling.

results.desc: Lupita, 56, Mexico City, Catholic. She goes to Mass every Sunday, cooks for the family, and her life is steady, but everything feels a little flat and grey this season. Just the day-to-day: the house, the cooking, the same routine
Polite and distant, like a neighbour I only wave to
Wake me up, or Give me back the spark. 'I miss You' is a bit more emotional than she feels, but it is the nearest.

friction.note: No word covers a dry, grey season: flat, dull, going through the motions. 'Numb' sounds like shock or depression, and 'At peace' and 'Worn out' do not fit either. A steady person who has simply lost the colour has nothing to tap.
'Nothing in particular' feels like a shrug. Someone whose life is routine might want 'The daily routine' or 'Home and family, the usual'.

'Just there, in the background' is close but a bit passive. Wording like 'Distant, polite' would name the dryness more exactly. The list is otherwise good and does not preach.

results.overall: For a steady Catholic in a grey season, the quiz was quick and felt gentle, and the people and God questions landed well. But the emotion words assume either pain or joy, so her real state, flat and going through the motions (spiritual dryness), had to be forced into 'Numb' and 'Nothing in particular'. No follow-up question applied to her answers.

verdict.why: Lupita's heart is not broken and she is not longing for anything. God has just become a polite neighbour she waves to while she goes through the Sunday routine. "God has slipped into the background" says exactly that, in her own sort of words, and she would recognise herself at once. The second half, "you want to wake your soul up to Him again", goes a little past her, because she hasn't put that wish into words yet. "Bless the LORD, O my soul" is a person talking to their own sleepy soul, which is what she needs. The turn at 103:2, "do not forget all His kind deeds", points her steady life (her family, her kitchen, her Mass) back at God as gifts rather than chores. Athanasius's advice, to give thanks through everything and stir up your own soul, reads to her as a warm invitation, not a correction. As a Catholic who knows the Fathers are trusted, she would like that it comes from him. Line 3, "worn you down until you feel empty and listless", would have made her life sound worse than it is and felt like a misreading. Line 2, the longing for God's house, is not where she is: she is in God's house every week and feels little there. The order puts the right line first, so she is never shown the heavier ones.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounds her. There is one small risk. If the result page leans too hard on "you should be more grateful", a woman who already serves her family every day could hear it as a scolding that her flatness is ingratitude. The page should present Psalm 103 as waking her soul with memory of God's kindness, not as a duty she has been failing.
verdict.theirSituation: Lupita's life is steady and her faith is dutiful but has gone flat and grey. God feels distant and polite. She isn't in pain; she simply isn't awake to Him, and she hasn't yet said to herself that she wants that to change.

results.desc: Kwame, 40, Accra, Methodist. He has an offer for a nursing job in Canada that would pay far more, but it means leaving his aging father and uprooting his wife and kids. He keeps changing his mind and has been asking God for a clear sign that has not come.

A big decision, and the people it affects (it is my future, but it is just as much about my father and my family)
An opportunity, but I don't know yet if it's from Him

Kwame has no enemy, only a hard choice, so those verses won't fit his situation. They won't hurt him, but a short framing note would help. verdict.theirSituation: A father torn over emigrating for work, praying for guidance that hasn't come.

results.desc: Rachel, 27, Singapore, evangelical. Work is good, her friends are good, she is still in her small group, but for months praying has felt like talking to the ceiling. She is not in crisis and she has not stopped believing; she just misses when it felt real.

answers.wanted: Good, but something's missing with God. 'Fine on the outside, not on the inside' sounds a bit more dramatic than how she feels. 'Good' leaves out the dryness.

'Silent. I pray and nothing changes' assumes the prayer is asking for an outcome. For someone whose prayer feels hollow, not unanswered, the second half does not fit. 'I've drifted from Him' could feel like blame for someone who is still showing up every week.
No follow-up is asked of someone in her situation. Nothing asks whether this is dryness or distance, or how long it has lasted, so the quiz may not tell this apart from real doubt or pulling away.

Line 2 is the closest: something is uneasy and won't settle. But it describes a mood, and her problem isn't a mood. God feels absent, and she isn't weighed down. She would tap yes to line 2 out of recognition, not because she felt fully seen. Line 3 (empty, listless, worn down) is wrong for her, because her life is going well. Psalm 42 turns out to be exactly her psalm: "My soul thirsts for God... When shall I come and appear before God?" and "Where is your God?" The result would speak to her more deeply than the line that led her to it. The verses shown are 42:5 and 42:11 ("Why are you downcast"), and they frame her as depressed. The deer-panting and thirst verses (42:1-2) are the ones that would make her say "that's me."
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounding. Calling her "downcast" and "weighed down" slightly overstates things. She said plainly that she isn't in crisis, and "Why are you downcast, O my soul?" as the headline verse could make her feel she's being called depressed. If the 988 crisis line appears on this path, it would misread her.
verdict.theirSituation: Her life is fine and her faith is intact, but for months God has felt absent in prayer, and she misses feeling that He is near. None of the three lines names this spiritual dryness. It needs a line like "You still believe, but God feels far away and you miss Him," leading to Psalm 42 with 42:1-2 shown first.

results.desc: Alasdair, 65, Perth, Scotland, Church of Scotland. A chapter ended well, and I'm not sure what the next one is

The old collie that won't have many more walks has nowhere to go. 'Someone I love' sounds like a person, and 'Someone or something I've lost' is premature because she is still alive. He would like something like 'An animal I love' or 'Something I'm about to lose'.

verdict.why: My real question right now is "what does God want me to do with the years I have left?" That is something I can't settle on my own, so line 1 is the one I'd tap. Line 2 about thanks is also true of me, but it's the smaller part. The verses given, 143:8 "Teach me the way I should walk" and 143:10 "Teach me to do Your will", are almost word for word my prayer, and a Kirk man would recognise them. I'm not in distress, so most of it doesn't sound like me, and "like those long dead" lands a bit close for a man my age who is watching his old dog fade. The result needs to say plainly that verses 8 and 10 are the part meant for me and the rest belongs to David's own trouble. Otherwise I'd wonder whether the quiz thinks I'm in a darker place than I am. It also misses that I'm grateful, which is half of how I feel. A short line saying "and alongside this, Psalm 103" would have caught it.
verdict.theirSituation: A newly retired man who is grateful but has no direction, and is asking God to show him what his remaining years are for while quietly facing the loss of his old dog.

results.desc: Jasmine, 22, Atlanta, grew up in a Baptist church in rural Georgia. She moved to the city in August for her first real job, lives alone for the first time, and is still working out where to buy groceries and who her friends will be. She has tried two churches and has not found one yet, and God feels like part of home she has not unpacked.

answers.wanted: Settling into a new place, or finding my people
Everyone I know is back home, and I haven't met many people here yet
Like part of home I haven't unpacked yet. Not gone, just on pause.
Help me find my place here (sits between 'I miss You' and 'Show me the way')
