friction.note: 'What's behind the good?' assumes things are good. She said up and down, lonely and unsure, and only got this question because something new is starting. New isn't the same as good, so it feels like being told to look on the bright side. 'A new home, or a new family' nearly fits, but 'new family' sounds like marriage or a baby, so she'd skip it.

There's no option for moving somewhere new or making friends from scratch. 'People in my life' sounds like people she already has, and she has hardly anyone here, so she has to pick 'What's next for me' instead.

'Far away, or gone' puts family who are simply back home next to people who have died or cut you off. It feels heavier than her situation. There's also no option for 'I don't really have people here yet'.

The options are either guilt ('I've drifted from Him') or flat ('Just there, in the background'). Nothing fits 'God isn't gone, I just haven't found a church or a routine here yet'. 'Drifted' would feel like a small judgment on someone who is simply between churches.
This is fine, and there are lots of options. But the ones for her situation are split across 'I miss You', 'Show me the way' and 'Help.', and none of them says 'help me find my place'.

results.overall: It was quick and friendly on a phone, and most of it made sense to her. But the quiz seems built for trouble or for things going well, and not for a big but ordinary change like moving away and living alone for the first time. She kept picking the nearest option and ended on a question that took for granted things were good.

verdict.why: Line 1 almost catches me, because I've been trying churches and I miss my church back home. But "long for... the home with Him that lasts forever" is about heaven and faint-with-longing devotion, and that isn't where I am. I'm not aching for God's courts. I just haven't gotten around to Him since the move. Line 2 names it plainly: God slipped into the background while I was figuring out groceries and friends, and part of me wants to wake that back up. It doesn't scold me. Psalm 103's "do not forget all His kind deeds" feels like a gentle nudge from home, and it lands. What it misses is the loneliness: the new city, living alone, not having friends yet. The result treats this as a drift in my attention to God and says nothing about the move or the church search that caused it. Line 3 would have felt too heavy. I'm unsettled, but not downcast.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounds. The only small misread is ranking Psalm 84 first. For someone church-shopping, "God's house" pulls at you, but the heaven-longing framing could make her briefly feel she's supposed to be more fervent than she is.
verdict.theirSituation: She's young and newly moved. She isn't in crisis and isn't hungry for heaven. God got packed away with the rest of home in the move, and she's lonely, looking for a church and friends, and would like to find her way back to Him.

results.desc: Nikos, 48, Thessaloniki, Greek Orthodox. His daughter is waiting on her university entrance results and his mother has a follow-up scan next week, so there is a low hum of worry under an otherwise normal routine. He says the Jesus Prayer when he cannot sleep and trusts things will probably be fine.

answers.wanted: Normal routine, but with a low worry underneath
Waiting on news (results, a scan)
Lord, have mercy.
I'm waiting on news about them (my mother's scan, my daughter's results)
Nothing is especially good. I just trust it will probably be fine

friction.note: Waiting is the most common low-grade worry, and none of the options covers it. 'About the same' hides it completely.
There is no 'Lord, have mercy' or 'Have mercy on me'. It is the most natural prayer for an Orthodox person (the Jesus Prayer), and 'Help.' is only a rough stand-in.
The question assumes a single 'them', but he has two people on his mind. 'Ill, or in danger' overstates a follow-up scan and does not fit exam results at all.
Picking 'Hopeful' triggered 'What's behind the good?', which assumes things are good. He is hopeful about how things will turn out, not happy about his life, so the question feels presumptuous.
'Quiet and ordinary' and 'Fine on the outside, not on the inside' are too far apart. He needs a middle option like 'Normal, with something hanging over me'.

results.overall: Quick and mostly easy. The core questions fitted him well, but the quiz has no idea of 'waiting on news'. It misread his hope as 'good', and the Orthodox prayer he actually says is missing from the list.

verdict.why: Line 1 overshoots. I am not "living afraid", and I don't need talking out of fear. I trust it will probably be fine. Line 2 is close, because I do pray for my mother's scan. But "you want words to pray with" misses: I already have them, the Jesus Prayer at night. Line 3 is the honest one. Nothing is wrong yet, but something uneasy sits under the routine and won't settle until the results and the scan come back. "Or uneasy" is what lets me say yes. Psalm 42 fits how I actually hold it: I talk to my own soul and put my hope in God. That is close to what I do at 3 a.m. with the prayer rope. Knowing that Athanasius, a Father of our Church, prescribed it, and that someone read him in Greek, makes me trust it more than an app's opinion.
verdict.wouldHurt: It wouldn't wound me, but two things jar a little. First, "weighed down" and "downcast" are heavier than my low hum. Printed in full, Psalm 42 has "my tears have been my food day and night" and "Where is your God?", and that reads like someone in real anguish. Second, the numbering: in my Church this is Psalm 41 and Psalm 91 is Psalm 90. Seeing only the Western numbers, next to a Greek Father, feels slightly foreign. Please show the Septuagint number too.
verdict.theirSituation: He is mildly worried while he waits on his daughter's exam results and his mother's scan, and he is basically calm and trusting. He is not afraid, grieving or pleading. He wants something for the low-grade unease of waiting.

results.desc: Mason, 15, Philadelphia, Catholic. His parents make him go to confirmation class on Wednesdays and he mostly finds it boring, though he liked one conversation about whether God cares about small stuff. Life is school, basketball and his phone, and God is something he has not thought about much.

answers.wanted: Fine / chill, or honestly 'Bored'. Happy is a bit strong, and worn out only means after practice.
School and basketball. There's no option for sports, hobbies or friends, so school was the nearest.
Something like 'Do You even care about the small stuff?' That's the one question I've actually wondered about. Otherwise 'Nothing, really' is honest.
'Just normal stuff: friends, basketball, nothing big.' Every option is about God or a big life event (new home, coming to faith, a chapter ending), and none of them is why things are fine for me.

friction.note: 'What's behind the good?' assumes there's a reason. Most options are spiritual ('I can see Him leading me', 'Coming back to Him', 'Coming to faith') or adult life events ('A new home, or a new family'). A kid whose life is just okay has nothing to tap except 'I'm not sure yet', and tapping it feels like failing the question.

There's no plain 'Fine', 'Bored' or 'Chill', which is how most teens would describe themselves. The list leans heavy (Ashamed, Bitter, Numb), so a normal kid gets pushed toward 'Happy' or 'At peace', and those feel like overclaiming.
There's no sports, hobbies, friends or phone/games option. 'Work or school' sounds like it was written for adults. 'God, and my faith' stands out as the obvious 'right answer' option.

'If you could say one thing to Him right now' assumes you already talk to God. For someone who doesn't, most options ('Stay with me', 'I miss You', 'How great You are', 'Make me who You want me to be') sound like church answers. 'Nothing, really' is the only honest tap, and it feels a bit like admitting you're a bad Catholic.
'This stretch of your life' is adult phrasing. A 15-year-old would say 'How's life lately?'
'Upset with me, and with reason' is a strange, confession-like phrase that a teen would read twice. 'A real gift' also sounds churchy.
This is fine overall and 'Just there, in the background' fit well. Only 'Displeased with me' and 'Clearly at work' read as preachy.

results.overall: Quick and mostly easy to tap through, and the God question had an honest answer for him. But the quiz is built for someone going through something or someone already religious. A bored, basically fine teenager kept hunting for 'fine / normal / basketball' and ended up forced into spiritual-sounding or too-strong options, especially on 'What's behind the good?'.

verdict.why: Line 1 isn't me. I'm not empty or worn down. I've got school, basketball and my phone, and I'm fine, so I'd tap "Not quite" right away. Line 2 gets the first half right: God really is in the background for me. But "wake your soul up to Him again" assumes He used to be in the front, and that I'm the one who wants Him back. Mostly my parents want that. I'd still tap yes, because it's the closest and I'm curious. Psalm 103's "do not forget all His kind deeds" connects a little to the one confirmation class I liked, about whether God cares about small stuff. It doesn't grab me, but it isn't wrong. It would help more if the line fit someone who never really thought about God, not only someone drifting back.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounds. "Again" and "you want to" quietly assume a faith and a longing that a teenager whose parents make him go may not have, so the result can read like it's about someone more religious than me.
verdict.theirSituation: A 15-year-old whose life is fine and busy, and who never really thought about God. He's in confirmation because his parents make him go, and he's only a little curious, mainly about whether God cares about small, everyday things.

results.desc: Camila, 31, Santiago, Chile, raised Catholic. She has not been to Mass in over a year, not because of anything dramatic, just work, weekends and a few podcasts that made her wonder whether any of it is true. She still says a quick prayer on the plane and feels mildly guilty, but mostly she just drifts.

answers.wanted: Something like 'a bit guilty' or 'drifting'. 'Ashamed' is far too strong for a quick plane prayer and a skipped Mass, so she settles for Unsure plus Restless.
Work is what fills her days, but what nags at her is 'whether any of it is true'. 'God, and my faith' sounds too devout for how she would put it.
'I don't know what to say' or 'Is any of this real?'. 'Are You there?' is the nearest; 'Nothing, really' felt too dismissive and 'I'm sorry' too heavy.

friction.note: There is no mild word for low-level guilt. 'Ashamed' is the only guilt word and it is too dramatic for a lapsed Catholic who just drifts, so her guilt goes unrecorded.
Intellectual doubt (podcasts making her wonder if it is true) has nowhere to go except 'God, and my faith', which sounds like a question for someone who is already devout.

The stem 'And God, right now, feels…' takes for granted that He is there to feel like anything. The 'I'm not sure He's there' option softens that, but someone doubting could read the question as assuming the answer.
Every option addresses Him as 'You'. For someone who is not sure anyone is listening, the question feels like being asked to pray in order to answer. A neutral 'I don't know what I'd say' would help.
With fifteen options the list is long on a phone. 'How great You are.' and 'Make me who You want me to be.' read as church language to a lapsed person.

results.overall: Quick and mostly painless. Camila could place herself as 'busy, drifted', but the quiz has no gentle words for low-level guilt or for 'I'm not sure it's true', so her answers come out slightly more religious or dramatic than she really feels.

verdict.why: Camila would stop at line 1. Its first half, "God has slipped into the background", describes her exactly: she didn't leave over anything dramatic, He just faded behind work and weekends. The second half, "you want to wake your soul up to Him again", goes a little past where she is. She feels guilty and not quite interested, rather than actively wanting to return. But she is taking a Christian quiz and still prays on planes, so she would accept it as close enough. Line 2 ("weighed down or uneasy") doesn't fit, because she isn't anguished, just drifting. Psalm 103's "Bless the LORD, O my soul... do not forget all His kind deeds" reads as a warm invitation, not a scolding. "Do not forget" names her drift without accusing her. What it doesn't touch is her real sticking point: the podcasts made her wonder whether any of this is true. The psalm and Athanasius both assume belief and call for thanks, so her quiet doubt goes unaddressed. She would feel mostly seen and gently nudged, but not fully met.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounding. The only small risk: "you want to wake your soul up to Him" and "we ought to give thanks... through everything" assume a desire and a certainty she isn't sure she has. Someone drifting because of doubt could read that as being told what she should feel, which would add a little to the guilt she already carries.
verdict.theirSituation: She is a lapsed Catholic drifting away through busyness and quiet intellectual doubt, not through pain. She feels a faint guilt but isn't sure she wants to come back, or that any of it is true.

results.desc: Steve, 58, Manchester, UK, came back to church in recovery. He gets his five-year sobriety chip next week, his daughter is coming to the meeting, and he is working again. He feels steady and thankful, and he talks to God most mornings as someone who stuck with him.

answers.wanted: My recovery: staying sober, and my five years coming up next week
He stuck with me, and I've stayed sober one day at a time

friction.note: There's nothing about recovery, addiction or a milestone. The nearest is 'Something I've done', and that reads as guilt, not as an achievement, so someone in recovery would steer clear of it. A 'Something I'm proud of / a milestone' option would fit.

'His kindness, to me and to everyone' is two ideas in one; Steve would tap 'to me' but stop at 'to everyone'. 'Coming back to Him' doesn't say when: he came back years ago, so he can't tell if it still counts. Nothing fits 'He didn't give up on me' or 'staying sober'.
'We're finding our way back to each other' fits very well for a daughter he is reconnecting with. No problems.
Fine. 'Thank You.' is exactly right. None of the options sound preachy to him.

results.overall: Quick and mostly natural. Steve could answer honestly and it felt like a chat, not a sermon. The one gap is that the biggest thing in his life, five years sober, has no option, so he had to go the long way round through 'Someone I love' and 'I'm growing'.

verdict.why: As Steve, the first line is him: steady, grateful, and talking to God most mornings as the One who stuck with him. "You want to thank God, in and through everything" fits a man about to get his five-year chip with his daughter there. "In and through everything" also covers the bad years he came through, not only the good week. Psalm 103 fits a man in recovery unusually well: "do not forget all His kind deeds," then forgiveness, healing, and a life redeemed "from the pit." He would feel seen, not flattered. The Songs of Ascents line is close, but "climbing" reads more like effort and striving than the settled thankfulness he has now, so the first line is the right one to come first. One small note: "in and through everything" is a bit of a church phrase, but it is short and plain enough that he would get it at once.

results.desc: Wanjiru, 31, Nairobi, Catholic. Her first baby, a son, was born six weeks ago, and she is running on very little sleep but keeps staring at him amazed. God feels close in a simple way, mostly thanks whispered during night feeds.

answers.wanted: Exhausting but wonderful: I'm barely sleeping but it's the best thing that's happened to me

friction.note: There is no option for a stretch that is both hard and wonderful, which is what having a newborn is. 'Good' leaves out the exhaustion and 'Hard, but I'm getting by' leaves out the joy. 'Up and down' sounds like mood swings, not joy and exhaustion at once. Something like 'Tiring, but wonderful' would fit a lot of new parents, caregivers and people in new jobs.

The first four options are about suffering, danger, need and loss, so a happy reason reads like an afterthought until she reaches 'They're new in my life'. It is a small thing, but she would scroll past four sad options first.
'A new home, or a new family' works for her, but 'family' sits oddly next to 'home'. 'A new baby, or a new family' or just 'A new family' would make it clearer that a birth counts.

results.overall: This was quick and warm, and most of the options named her life exactly: worn out and grateful, God close, 'Thank You', someone new in her life. The one jolt was the first question, which made her choose between hard and good when her life right now is both.

verdict.why: Thanks whispered during night feeds is the centre of my life right now, so "You want to thank God, in and through everything" is the first line that is me, and I'd say yes to it. Psalm 103 speaks to me: "Bless the LORD, O my soul, and do not forget all His kind deeds" is exactly what I'm doing at 3am. Further in, "As a father has compassion on his children" and the mercy "to children's children" would land hard with a newborn in my arms. It doesn't mention the amazement at my son, or the exhaustion, so it feels a little general. Line 2 ("something new has begun in your home") actually comes closer to the baby, but its psalm talks about foes and sackcloth, which isn't me. So I'm glad the thanks line came first.
verdict.theirSituation: A tired new mother, amazed by her six-week-old son, whose prayer is simple thanks during night feeds. The line fits the thanks but not the newness of the baby or her exhaustion.

results.desc: Budi, 35, Jakarta, Protestant. He was just promoted to lead his team at a logistics firm after years of hard work, and his parents are very proud. He is grateful and a little wary of getting too pleased with himself, and wants to handle the new power well.

answers.wanted: Grateful, and a little careful not to get proud. None of the words covers that wariness. 'Unsure' and 'Anxious' go too far.

Thank You, and keep me humble. What he most wants to say is to help him use this new authority well. 'Show me the way' and 'Make me who You want me to be' come near it, but neither is about handling power.
Years of work paying off: a promotion, a new responsibility. No option is about a new role or being trusted with more. 'I can see Him leading me' was the nearest.

friction.note: Every word here is either a pleasant feeling or a distress. There is no word for a sober, watchful kind of good, such as 'humbled' or 'careful'. A man who wants to stay humble is left choosing between plain happiness and anxiety.

The options lean toward church life ('Coming to faith', 'Coming back to Him') or toward home life ('A new home, or a new family'). None covers a new job or responsibility, which is one of the most common good things that happen to people. 'A chapter ending well' feels wrong for something that is just beginning.

Nothing lets a person ask for humility or wisdom in success. A new leader wanting to use power well is a situation the questions never quite reach, so the quiz may not be able to tell him apart from someone who is simply thankful.

results.overall: The quiz was quick and easy to follow, and most taps fitted a good season with something new starting. But what makes Budi's moment his own is the wish to stay humble with new power, and no question lets him say it. He would worry that his result will be a generic thanksgiving psalm.

verdict.why: Gratitude is the strongest thing I feel right now. After years of work, this promotion feels like God's kindness, and my parents are proud. "Thank God, in and through everything" is close enough that I'd tap yes right away. Psalm 103:2, "do not forget all His kind deeds", also quietly answers my worry about getting proud: remember where this came from. Further on, the psalm says man's days are like grass and speaks of fearing the Lord, which speaks to my wariness even though the quiz never asked about it. The second line, about the shepherd, is pleasant, but it describes being guided. I am in a moment of being given something, not of being led.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounds. If I had said "Not quite" to both lines, the fallback would feel wrong: its three choices are all about suffering (grinding down, weighing on me, afraid), and my situation is a good thing. Being routed there would feel like the quiz assumed something was wrong with my life.
verdict.theirSituation: He has just been given authority and blessing after years of work. He is thankful, and he wants to stay humble and use his new power well over the people he leads, which the line on gratitude alone does not name.

results.desc: Elena, 69, Toronto, Orthodox, born in Moldova. After twelve years of silence over their late mother's house, her brother called her at Easter and they had lunch together last month. She feels lighter than she has in a decade and keeps thanking God that it happened while they are both still alive.

answers.wanted: Something hard has healed, a long silence with my brother is over. 'Finally over' fits the twelve years, but it feels more like a mending than a trouble ending.
Twelve years of not speaking to my brother. 'A falling-out' sounds smaller and shorter than what it was.

He called, we made peace, and God made it happen. 'We made peace' is true, but it leaves God out, and I thank Him for it every day. The options that credit God are all about rescue or correction, and none of those fit.

friction.note: 'A falling-out' reads as a small quarrel. For a family estrangement that lasted years, something like 'A long estrangement' or 'Years of not speaking' would fit better.

No option has both people reconciling and God's hand in it. She would want something like 'We made peace, and I know God brought it about'. Having to pick between 'We made peace' and God-centred rescue options feels like a false choice.

'Something hard is finally over' assumes hardship. When a long rift ends in reconciliation it feels like a gift or a healing, not just an ending. She tapped it, but she'd have liked a 'Something has been healed' option.
Being asked 'What was it?' after a joyful answer is fine. But the list opens with 'People who were against me' and 'Trouble on every side', which set a darker tone than her story has.

results.overall: Quick and warm: the core questions fit a thankful, reconciled person well, and 'We're finding our way back to each other' felt written for her. The follow-ups about how it ended made her joy sound like the end of a fight, with a smaller word for twelve years of silence than she'd use and no way to say both 'we made peace' and 'God did it'.

verdict.why: Elena is full of gratitude that God let her and her brother make peace while they are both alive. "You want to thank God" is exactly where she is, and she would tap yes right away. Psalm 103, with "do not forget all His kind deeds," fits her very well. The rest of the psalm fits too: "He will not always strive with us," and a life that is short like grass. That speaks straight to twelve lost years and to her sense of time running out. The line says "in and through everything," which is a bit broad for her. Her thanks is for one specific mercy, not a general habit. But it doesn't box her in. She would feel seen and warmed.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing would wound her. One thing may puzzle her. As an Orthodox woman she knows the Septuagint numbering, so "Bless the Lord, O my soul" (this psalm) is Psalm 102 to her. At Vespers, "Psalm 103" is the creation psalm that opens with the same words. Seeing "Psalms 103 and 104" printed in Hebrew numbering, under a Greek Father's name, could make her think the wrong psalm was shown. Consider a small note giving the Septuagint number.
verdict.theirSituation: Elena made peace with her brother after twelve years of silence over their late mother's house, and she is thanking God that it happened while they are both still alive.

results.desc: Luis, 26, Quetzaltenango, Guatemala, evangelical. His mother's heart surgery went well two weeks ago after months of the whole family praying and saving for it. He feels like God actually heard them, and he wants to remember this feeling when things are hard again.

answers.wanted: Really good now, after a really hard few months
My mom's illness and surgery. The option reads as if it was my own illness

friction.note: There's no way to say 'hard for months, good now'. Picking 'Really good' leaves out the long, hard stretch that makes this gratitude mean so much.
'What was it?' with 'An illness, or a scare' sounds like it was about me. It should make clear it can be someone I love, like 'An illness or a scare (mine or someone's)'.

I never got this question because my trend was 'Something hard is finally over'. But 'An answered prayer' is exactly what's behind the good for me, so it's a shame I'm not asked. Also, nothing lets me say I want to remember this feeling for when things get hard again, and that's my main reason for coming.
Both 'Someone I love' and 'God, and my faith' fit. Picking one felt a little like a box.

results.overall: It was quick and felt natural. Most options fit a grateful 'God answered our prayers' moment well. The only rough spots were that the illness question assumes it was my own, and there's nowhere to say I want to keep this memory for hard days.

verdict.why: Months of praying, then the surgery went well, and he feels God heard them: that is "you ran to God, He brought you through". Evangelicals share testimonies, so "tell people what He did" rings true too. Psalm 46:1 ("an ever-present help in times of trouble") is exactly the verse he would want to hold onto when things get hard again, so the result speaks to his wish to remember. The one small miss is that his deepest wish is to remember, not mainly to tell. Line 2's Psalm 103:2 ("do not forget all His kind deeds") speaks to that remembering even more directly, so he might have been as happy or happier there. Still, he would say yes to line 1 without hesitating.
verdict.theirSituation: His mother's heart surgery went well after months of family prayer and saving, and he wants to thank God and hold onto this memory of God's faithfulness for the next hard season.

results.desc: Dorothy, 80, Tuscaloosa, Alabama, United Methodist. Her days are quiet: her garden, her Sunday school class, calls with grandchildren, and a walk when her knees allow. She is content, not dramatic about it, and feels God has been kind to her over a long life.

answers.wanted: My family and grandchildren. 'People in my life' is near enough, but 'Someone I love' is singular and neither quite says family

'He's been good to me all my life.' She would think of a long life of kindness, not a new event. 'His kindness, to me and to everyone' is closest, though the 'and to everyone' part is more than she means

friction.note: 'Quiet and ordinary' and 'Good' both fit her. A contented older person has to choose between them, and 'ordinary' can sound a little like settling. Something like 'Quiet and good' or 'Content' would suit her.

'What's behind the good?' is odd phrasing on a first read. It also assumes something recent caused it. Most options are events (an answered prayer, a new home, coming to faith, a chapter ending), and nothing fits a lifetime of steady blessing.
'Clear my name.' would puzzle her with no context. 'Nothing, really.' reads strangely as something to say to God.
There is no plain 'My family' option. For an 80-year-old whose mind is on grandchildren, that is the obvious answer.

The option key says 'heavy' but the label says 'Sad'. That is fine for her; she only sees 'Sad'. The list is long on a phone, but the good words are at the bottom, so a content person has to scroll past a lot of trouble first.

results.overall: It went quickly and felt gentle. Most questions had an answer that fit her. The quiz does lean toward trouble, though: it opens with hard options and has few ways to say 'my life is steadily good, thank the Lord.' She might wonder whether it was built for people with something wrong.

verdict.why: Dorothy is quietly grateful and feels God has been kind to her over a long life. "You want to thank God, in and through everything" says that simply, and she would tap yes at once. Psalm 103 is one she likely already knows from her King James and Methodist hymns ("Bless the LORD, O my soul... forget not all his benefits"). The psalm fits her age well: it talks about God healing, crowning a life with lovingkindness, and our days being like grass while His mercy lasts from everlasting. That is comforting to her, not grim. Line 2 (Psalm 145) would also have suited her, so either result lands.

results.desc: Thandi, 17, Cape Town, Anglican. Last Sunday she watched her best friend, who had not grown up in church, get baptised, and she cried more than she expected. It made her own faith feel new again, and she has been reading the Psalms before bed.

answers.wanted: Something old feels new again: my faith feels fresh, but nothing has actually started
Moved, or stirred up. I cried at the baptism and none of the words quite say that tender, full feeling

friction.note: 'Something new is starting' sounds like a new job or a move. Faith feeling new again is more like a renewal, so she paused over 'Getting better' against 'new'. An option like 'Something feels new again' would fit.
There is no word for being moved or touched, the crying-at-church feeling. Grateful and Hopeful are near, but she would look for 'Moved' first.
She was torn between 'God, and my faith' and 'Someone I love', because the trigger was her friend's baptism. The pick-one limit makes her split something that is really one thing.
'Coming to faith, mine or someone else's' fits so exactly that it almost gives the quiz away, but it doesn't feel pushy. A 17-year-old would just be pleased to see it.

results.overall: Quick and easy on a phone, and it felt warm, not preachy. Most taps were obvious for her good, renewed season. The only snags were the missing word for being 'moved' and 'something new is starting' not quite matching faith feeling new again.

verdict.why: Line 2 describes exactly what happened to me: I watched my best friend get baptised and cried at how much God loves us. Athanasius telling me to sing Psalm 32 over people being baptised feels like he's talking about last Sunday, and that would give me chills. Line 1 is true in a general way. I am grateful and I've been reading the Psalms. But it's vague, and something almost anyone would agree with, so I'd tap "Not quite" hoping for something closer. There is a real risk, though. Someone less patient, or someone who doesn't know a better line is coming, could accept line 1 and miss the result that actually names what they lived through. The line that fits an event this closely should probably come first.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounding. Two small things: "the corruption we are born into" is heavy wording to hear about my friend on her happy day, but as an Anglican I know what baptism means, so it doesn't sting. And the middle of Psalm 32, about keeping silent and bones wasting away, is about someone confessing their own sin, not about joy watching someone else. Reading it in full, I'd need the advice line to remind me why I was given it.
verdict.theirSituation: A 17-year-old whose own faith feels new again after watching her unchurched best friend get baptised.

results.desc: Joseph, 45, Kochi, Kerala, Syro-Malabar Catholic. His family just moved into the first flat they have ever owned, after years of renting and moving for his work. The priest came to bless it on Saturday, and he feels settled and grateful for the first time in a long while.

answers.wanted: My family and our new home. None of the options covers home or settling in, so 'People in my life' was the nearest. 'Nothing in particular' felt wrong because the flat really is on his mind.

friction.note: There is no option for home, family or where I live. For someone whose big news is a house or a move, the focus question feels like it has nothing to do with him. 'People in my life' sounds like other people causing trouble, not his own wife and children.

'A new home, or a new family' pairs two different things. He would tap it for the flat, but he stopped for a second to wonder whether 'new family' meant a wedding or a baby. 'A new home' could be its own option.
He might also have wanted 'An answered prayer', since owning a home was something the family prayed about for years. He can only pick one, so he chose the more concrete option.
'Good' and 'Really good' are close together. A settled, grateful man who isn't given to exaggerating picks 'Good', and he may wonder whether that choice changes much.

results.overall: The quiz was quick and pleasant, and the happy answers were easy to give. The one gap was that his main subject, the new home and his family, had no place until the last follow-up. At that point 'A new home' felt like the quiz had finally understood him.

verdict.why: Line 1 is true of Joseph right now. He is grateful, and a devout Syro-Malabar Catholic would read "thank God, in and through everything" and say yes straight away, so he taps it before he ever sees line 2. Line 2 is the exact match, though: a new home, just blessed by the priest, given to God with thanks. It is almost a description of his Saturday, and Psalm 30's heading ("at the dedication of the house") would have felt made for him. Psalm 103 ("Bless the LORD, O my soul, and do not forget all His kind deeds") still speaks to him warmly and fits his mood, so the result helps, but it is the general answer when a specific one existed. The ranking should put the house-dedication line first when the answers point to a new home. A general gratitude line that sits above a specific one will catch nearly everyone who is thankful. In Psalm 30, "mourning into dancing" also fits his years of renting and moving. "Foes rejoicing" is a small odd note for him but nothing that would hurt.
verdict.theirSituation: After years of renting, Joseph has just moved his family into the first home they have ever owned, and a priest blessed it on Saturday. He is settled and grateful, and what he most wants is to give the home to God. That is exactly the second line, the one he never reaches.

results.desc: Dawit, 50, Addis Ababa, Ethiopian Orthodox. This month he made the last payment on a debt that had hung over him for seven years, just in time for Meskel. He feels free and wants to mark it somehow, and God feels like someone who carried him through a long road.

answers.wanted: Free, relieved: a weight is off my shoulders
Nothing to say about them; this was between me, my debt and God
He carried me the whole way
A debt, money trouble that hung over me for years
I kept working and paying, and He carried me through to the end

friction.note: No money or debt option, even though 'Money' is one of the focus choices. A seven-year debt is not really 'a long wait' or 'trouble on every side'. He has to squeeze it into a category that doesn't describe it.

None of the options covers years of his own effort with God carrying him through. 'He got me out' leaves out the work he did himself, 'It just passed' leaves out God, and 'I kept my head and got away' sounds like escaping enemies. Something like 'I kept going and He carried me' is missing.
There is no 'Relieved' or 'Free'. After paying off a long debt, that is the first word he would reach for.

'What's behind the good?' is skipped because the trend was 'over'. Yet he feels grateful and wants to mark the moment, so he would miss 'A chapter ending well' and has no way to say he wants to give thanks or celebrate (with Meskel coming).
The question assumes other people are part of what's going on. For a private money burden, 'Fine' is only a placeholder, and choosing it feels like skipping the question.

results.overall: Quick and mostly natural. The core questions let him say he is grateful and at the end of a hard road. The follow-ups about how it ended are built for enemies, illness or falling-outs, so his plain but huge relief at paying off a debt had to be squeezed into 'a long wait' and 'He got me out'.

verdict.why: As Dawit I would say yes to the first line. What I feel most is thankfulness. I would also say it the way my Church does: the Ethiopian liturgy opens with the Prayer of Thanksgiving, which thanks God for everything, so "in and through everything" sounds like my own prayer. The line is a bit general, though. It says nothing about the long road or the burden being lifted, so it reads as "near enough" rather than "exactly". The second line is actually closer to my story: He brought me through, and I want to mark it and tell people. But I would already have said yes before I reached it. Psalm 103 is a very good result for me. Its opening lines, "forget not all His benefits... who redeems your life from the pit... your youth is renewed like the eagle's", speak straight to a man who has just been freed from seven years of debt. I would feel seen and lifted, and I might read it aloud at home for Meskel. Psalm 46, if I had got to it, is more about refuge while the danger is still around you than about thanks once it is over, so it would suit me less.
verdict.theirSituation: A long hardship has just ended in deliverance. He is grateful and wants to mark it, and that "carried through and set free" part is sharper than a general wish to give thanks in everything.

results.desc: Karen, 39, Seattle, non-denominational. After a long stretch of being single and making peace with it, she got engaged in August to a man she met through a friend at church. She is happy, a bit stunned, and keeps telling God she did not see this coming.

answers.wanted: Surprised, or stunned. The biggest feeling is 'I did not see this coming', and there's no word for that
My engagement, or the wedding and my life with him. 'Someone I love' and 'What's next for me' are each half of it
Something like 'I didn't see this coming' or 'You surprised me.' Thank You is true, but it misses the amazement
We're getting married. 'They're new in my life' is mostly right, but he's more than a new person now
Something I'd stopped hoping for. 'A new home, or a new family' sounds like moving house or having a baby. 'An answered prayer' doesn't fit either, because she had stopped asking

friction.note: The list has no word for surprise or awe ('Stunned', 'Amazed'). For someone whose good news came out of nowhere, that is the main feeling.
There's no option for a new relationship or an engagement. 'Someone I love' is next to options about suffering and loss, so it feels like it's meant for sad situations.
Most options here are about suffering, danger, need or loss. A happy engaged person has to scan past a lot of grief to find 'They're new in my life'.

'A new home, or a new family' is vague. You can't tell whether it means marriage, moving house, adoption or a baby. There's also no option for a gift that came after you'd made peace with not having it, which is a very common story for single women in church.
The 15 options feel long on a phone. Half of them are laments, so on a joyful path the list feels heavy.

results.overall: Mostly smooth and quick for a happy person, and the core questions let her say 'really good, something new, God is at work, thank You' without strain. But the quiz has no words for surprise or for a relationship starting, so she keeps choosing things that are near enough rather than true.

verdict.why: Karen is overflowing with thanks, and Line 1 is close enough that she would tap "Yes, that's it" right away. Psalm 103 fits her well. "Do not forget all His kind deeds" is what she keeps saying to God. Further in, the psalm says God "satisfies you with good things" and "renews your youth like the eagle's", which lands for someone who waited a long time and had made peace with being single. The line's wording pulls a little the wrong way, though. "In and through everything" sounds like thanking God in spite of hard times. Her thanks is for one specific, surprising gift. Line 2 is about a new home. She might feel it points ahead to a shared home after the wedding, but that home hasn't started yet, so it would read as a near miss. It doesn't box her in or hurt her. It is just a bit generic: nothing picks up on "I didn't see this coming." A line like "Something good has come that you never expected, and you want to thank Him for it" would have made her feel truly seen.
verdict.theirSituation: She has just been given an unexpected good gift (an engagement after years of contented singleness), and her thanks is surprised, joyful gratitude for that one gift, not thanks through hard times.
